newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Desertification pact to enter into force this year.
newsitem.headline: Desertification pact to enter into force this year.

text.p: The Convention to Combat Desertification, designed to curb degradation of arid lands affecting more than one billion people worldwide, will enter into force on December 26, the United Nations said on Tuesday.
The environmental treaty, called for at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992 and adopted in June 1994, was ratified by Chad last week -- the 50th country to do so.
"This starts the 90-day countdown for the treaty's entry into force, which will take place on December 26," the Geneva-based interim secretariat said in a statement.
"The Convention will then become international law for all the countries that have ratified or acceded to it," it added.
The treaty commits signatory states to implement solid national commitments to combat erosion and soil degradation, and promotes a participatory approach involving grassroots groups.

Overcultivation and overgrazing, which lead to erosion and soil degradation, combined with deforestation and poor irrigation, are estimated to cost $42 billion a year in lost food production and other costs, according to the U.N.
Some 70 per cent of the 5.2 billion hectares of drylands used for agriculture around the world are already degraded. Thus, desertification affects nearly 30 per cent of the earth's total land area.
Africa and Asia are the worst hit economically, but some 74 per cent of U.S. drylands are severely or moderately affected. France, Greece, Italy, Spain and Portugal are also hit.
"In all, more than 110 countries have drylands that are potentially at risk," the statement said.
"The human cost is even higher. The livelihoods of more than a billion people are now at risk, and over 135 million may be in danger of being driven from their land," it added.
The first session of the Conference of the Parties, the body which will implement the pact, is scheduled to take place in late 1997 in Rome.
